catalog_quote: 2.121 Word Stress. This stress is characterized by length15 rather than by intensity or by pitch, and it falls normally on the last syllable of a grammatical word. As in SF, stressed syllables are generally longer than unstressed; however, the position of the stress is more unstable in LF.16 Indeed, the slightest insistence may shift the stress backward, toward the first syllable, e.g., il admirait /i 'lad mi re/ ... [it] is not unusual for a non-final grammatical word to retain its stress, thus creating doubly accentuated phonetic words, e.g., du bon temps /- ' '/, plusieurs jeunes /- ' '/. In such instances, the two stresses normally follow each other, the final stress moving backward, e.g., elles sont belles aussi /- - ' ' -/. Since intensity is not involved, the rhythmical unit is not split into two by the additional accent; however, the first stressed ... what reduced. Hence, it is the first stressed syllable that bears the primary stress, the final bearing the secondary. This produces a rhythmical pattern more akin to English than to French, which lacks, however, the intensity of English accentuation.19
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress (realised as length, not intensity or pitch) falls on the last syllable of the grammatical word, as in Standard French; but stress position is unstable: any insistence pulls it back toward the first syllable, non-final grammatical words often keep their stress (giving phonetic words with two adjacent stresses), and in such cases the first stressed syllable carries primary and the final syllable secondary stress, yielding a more English-like rhythm.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In doubly-accented phonetic words 'the first stressed syllable.. bears the primary stress, the final bearing the secondary' (p. 31); a separate intensity-based 'emphatic stress' (§2.122) exists and, unlike SF, does not always fall on the first consonant-initial syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress retracts toward the first syllable under 'the slightest insistence' (il admirait /i 'lad mi re/; Louisiana /'lu zjan/ beside /lwi zjan/); non-final grammatical words retain stress (du bon temps /- ' '/, plusieurs jeunes /- ' '/, elles sont belles aussi /- - ' ' -/); the authors elsewhere call LaF word stress 'extremely mobile' and mention 'perhaps free stress' as a possible English influence while insisting stress 'remains primarily French'. Book's summary passage: the stressed syllable(s) 'tend to be toward the center of the phonetic word'.
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for the grammatical word within the phonetic word / stress group (SF-style phrase-final stress with the LF innovation that non-final words keep stress); the description is of connected speech of Lafayette-area informants, not citation forms. §2.123 adds that LF has a substantially higher ratio of stresses per clause than SF.
new_statements.identity_note: Conwell & Juilland 1963 describe 'the Lafayette dialect (LaF), because a majority of our informants reside in Lafayette' (Lafayette Parish, Louisiana), i.e. one Acadian/Cajun French variety; Glottolog caju1236 (Louisiana French, frc) has no separate code for the Lafayette dialect. The other described varieties (Lafourche/Terrebonne: Papen & Rottet 1997, Oukada 1977, Blainey 2013; Ville Platte/Evangeline: Klingler & Lyche 2012; Swords: Sullivan 1977) all fall under the same glottocode. Two Glottolog-listed 'grammar sketch' refs (Felder et al. 2010 Heidelberger Korpus; Pitz 2004 Frankish/Romance) are misattributed and do not concern Louisiana French.
